title: Flora Hamilton
text:
I’m an environmental data scientist specializing in remote sensing and geospatial analytics in western landscapes.
I’m a Research Associate with the Ecosystem Management and Research Group at Colorado State University’s Natural Resource Ecology Laboratory (NREL). I bring together field observations, drone and satellite imagery, animal GPS data, and other ecological datasets to study landscape patterns and support evidence-based management.

title: Research Projects
text: I use remote sensing, field data, and spatial models to understand how western ecosystems respond to disturbance and management. These highlights include collaborative work from my roles at CSU NREL and NASA DEVELOP, alongside ongoing research; related and publically available technical reports are linked below.

title: Research Projects
text:
Highlighted project

Post-fire snowpack dynamics in the Colorado Front Range
How do burn severity and snow zone shape snow depth across the accumulation and melt seasons? My team and I combine airborne lidar, field observations, and terrain data to investigate this across two Front Range watershed using airborne Lidar and satellite imagery.
Manuscript in preparation.

title: Research Projects
text:
Other selected work


Quaking aspen after wildfire
Northern Colorado · 2025–2026
Mapping aspen occurrence with optical and radar imagery, terrain data, and spatially validated models.
Deliverable: Maps, models, code repo., technical report


Cattle movement and rangeland use
Rangelands · 2024–Present
Using GPS-collar data to study how cattle movement, behavior, and preferences vary across pastures and management treatments.


Virtual fencing and vegetation
Rangelands · 2024–2026
Four years of monitoring across 47 plots to examine vegetation patterns alongside climate and management.


Individual tree-crown mapping
New Mexico Highlands · 2025–Present
Resolving duplicate crowns at overlapping image-tile boundaries to improve a map product of individual tree crown and tree top detections in surviving tree islands across the New Mexico Highlands.


Vegetation monitoring
Western Rangelands · 2024–Present
Translating Line Point Intersect and datasets from other vegetation monitoring methods into insights about field conditions and management results.

title: About
text:
I’m a Research Associate with the Ecosystem Management and Research Group at Colorado State University’s Natural Resource Ecology Laboratory (NREL). My work supports ecological management research across western rangelands and forests. I combine field observations, drone and satellite imagery, animal GPS data, and geospatial, statistical, and machine-learning methods to study ecological patterns and management outcomes.
I’m interested in how environmental data can deepen our understanding of ecosystems and inform how people manage them. My background also includes applied research, contract project leadership, classroom teaching, and work with technology startups.

title: About
text:
Background
I grew up in Taiwan and Oregon, places with very different landscapes that shaped my curiosity about ecology. Taiwan’s mountains span subtropical lowland forests to temperate and alpine forests. Oregon’s high deserts, forests, and basalt landscapes offered another world to explore. Some of my favorite memories are amongst Taiwan’s mangroves, banyan trees, stag beetles, blue magpies, and Formosan macaques, as well as Oregon’s redwoods, salmonberries, and sturgeon in the Columbia River.
